claim: In the adult mouse basal forebrain, vGlut2+ neurons define a distinct population of excitatory neurons that do not overlap with cholinergic neurons.
source: In the adult mouse BF, vGlut2 +neurons define a distinct population of excitatory neurons that do not overlap with cholinergic neurons (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating spatial separation of vGlut2+ and ChAT+ neurons.

claim: Re-feeding after an overnight fast activated basal forebrain neurons as detected by increased expression of Fos.
source: Re-feeding after an overnight fast activated BF neurons as detected by increased expression of the immediate early gene product Fos (Figure 1A–B) (Herman et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by Fos immunohistochemistry data in Figure 1A-B and citation to Herman et al., 2016.

claim: There is an increase in the percentage of Fos+ vGlut2BF neurons in the fed state compared to periods of fasting.
source: Similar to cholinergic BF neurons, we observed an increase in the percentage of Fos+ VGlut2BF neurons in the fed state compared to periods of fasting (Figure 1A,C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating statistical difference between fasted and fed states.

claim: vGlut2BF neurons are a distinct cellular population apart from cholinergic neurons and are similarly activated by feeding.
source: These data indicate that vGlut2BF neurons are a distinct cellular population apart from cholinergic neurons, and are similarly activated by feeding.
evidence: Inference drawn from the Fos activation data and anatomical separation from cholinergic neurons.

claim: A population of vGlut2BF neurons is activated when fasted mice approached and interacted with food, prior to consummatory behavior.
source: We identified a population of activated vGlut2BF neurons when fasted mice approached and interacted with food, prior to consummatory behavior (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by in vivo calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Approximately 15.6% of DBB neurons were reactive to food odor alone.
source: Approximately 15.6% of DBB neurons were reactive to food odor alone, with 2.5% being responsive to not only food odors, but also other stimuli that included walking, grooming, or physical stimuli (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Quantification of neuronal responses shown in Figure 1G.

claim: 2.5% of DBB neurons were responsive to food odors and other stimuli including walking, grooming, or physical stimuli.
source: Approximately 15.6% of DBB neurons were reactive to food odor alone, with 2.5% being responsive to not only food odors, but also other stimuli that included walking, grooming, or physical stimuli (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Quantification of neuronal responses shown in Figure 1G.

claim: 9.4% of DBB neurons responded to other stimuli but not food.
source: 9.4% of neurons recorded responded to these other stimuli but not food, and the vast majority were unreactive or showed non-specific activation (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Quantification of neuronal responses shown in Figure 1G.

claim: vGlut2BF neurons expressing mNaChBac showed increased spontaneous frequencies, action potential half-widths, and action potential voltage thresholds.
source: First, by performing whole cell recordings 7–10 days after viral injection, we measured that vGlut2BF neurons that expressed mNaChBac showed increased spontaneous frequencies, action potential half-widths, and action potential voltage thresholds (Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2B-C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Current-injection ramps showed increased area under the activation curve in mNaChBac versus control neurons.
source: Current-injection ramps showed increase area under the activation curve in mNaChBac versus control neurons, indicating neuronal activation was sustained and mNaChBac expressing neurons are capable of increasing the excitability of downstream targets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: mNaChBac expressing neurons are capable of increasing the excitability of downstream targets.
source: Current-injection ramps showed increase area under the activation curve in mNaChBac versus control neurons, indicating neuronal activation was sustained and mNaChBac expressing neurons are capable of increasing the excitability of downstream targets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Inference based on the increased area under the curve during current injection experiments.

claim: Extracellular single-unit recordings confirmed increased spontaneous frequency in animals containing mNaChBac.
source: Using photostimulation as confirmation of electrode placement and cell identification, we recorded spontaneous activity in the basal forebrain, and confirmed increased spontaneous frequency in animals containing mNaChBac (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Approximately 4-5 days after viral injection with mNaChBac, mice began to precipitously lose weight while concurrently reducing their food intake.
source: Strikingly, approximately 4–5 days after viral injection, mice began to precipitously lose weight, while concurrently reducing their food intake (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: Supported by body weight and food intake measurements shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Experimental animals rapidly lost 30% of their initial body weight as food intake ceased, eventually leading to starvation and death within 9-12 days after viral injection.
source: Experimental animals rapidly lost 30% of their initial body weight as food intake ceased, eventually leading to starvation and death within 9–12 days after viral injection (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: Supported by survival curve and body weight data shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: Four days following viral delivery, animals did not show changes in pituitary hormones or peripherally circulating thyroid hormones T3 and T4.
source: We found no changes in pituitary hormones, or peripherally circulating thyroid hormones T3 and T4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by hormone measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: Animals did not show altered levels of glucose or insulin, indicating that hypo-insulinemia was not the cause of weight loss.
source: Furthermore, animals did not show altered levels of glucose or insulin, indicating that hypo-insulinemia was not the cause of weight loss (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by glucose and insulin measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Leptin levels were similar between experimental mice and controls, indicating that altered leptin signaling did not induce weight loss or decreased food intake.
source: Additionally, leptin levels were also similar between experimental mice and controls, indicating that altered leptin signaling did not induce weight loss or decreased food intake (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by leptin measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: mNaChBac injected animals exhibited elevated levels of ghrelin comparable to the fasted state.
source: Interestingly, mNaChBac injected animals exhibited elevated levels of ghrelin comparable to the fasted state, indicating ghrelin was indeed being released due to diminished food intake.
evidence: Supported by ghrelin measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Elevated ghrelin signaling was unable to induce feeding in mNaChBac injected animals, as mice continued to exhibit self-starvation.
source: However, elevated ghrelin signaling was unable to induce feeding, as mice continued to exhibit self-starvation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by ghrelin measurements and food intake data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The observed rapid weight loss in mice with increased vGlut2BF neuron activity was primarily due to diminished food intake, and not an altered metabolism.
source: Together, these data suggest that the observed rapid weight loss in mice with increased vGlut2BF neuron activity was primarily due to diminished food intake, and not an altered metabolism.
evidence: Inference based on the hormone panel data showing no metabolic dysfunction.

claim: Food supplementation via oral gavage 2x/day ameliorated the starvation phenotype.
source: Indeed, we found that food supplementation via oral gavage 2x/day ameliorated the starvation phenotype (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 2F comparing mNaChBac alone versus mNaChBac with gavage and liquid diet.

claim: Over-activity of vGlut2BF neurons leads to hypophagia-induced weight loss.
source: Together, these data further substantiate that over-activity of vGlut2BF neurons leads to hypophagia-induced weight loss.
evidence: Inference based on the rescue experiment with oral gavage and the hormone panel data.

claim: Mice treated with CNO displayed increased food intake compared to saline-treated controls in both ad libitum and fasted conditions.
source: In both scenarios, mice treated with CNO displayed increased food intake compared to saline-treated controls (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Supported by food intake measurements shown in Figure 3B-C following chemogenetic inhibition with hM4Di.

claim: vGlut2BF neurons and their associated circuits are potent drivers of appetite suppression.
source: Collectively, these data reveal a novel role for vGlut2BF in regulating food intake and identified this neuronal population and their associated circuits as potent drivers of appetite suppression.
evidence: Inference based on both activation and inhibition experiments showing bidirectional control of food intake.

claim: Mice with overactive vGlut2BF neurons via mNaChBac expression suppressed leptin deficiency-induced hyperphagia and dramatically reduced their food intake with subsequent weight loss.
source: Notably, we found that mice with overactive vGlut2BF neurons via mNaChBac expression suppressed leptin deficiency-induced hyperphagia, and dramatically reduced their food intake with subsequent weight loss (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: Supported by body weight and food intake data in Lepob/ob mice shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Food avoidance pathways driven by vGlut2BF neurons can over-ride robust intrinsic signaling mechanisms that govern feeding.
source: Together, these experiments reveal that food avoidance pathways driven by vGlut2BF neurons can over-ride robust intrinsic signaling mechanisms that govern feeding.
evidence: Inference based on the ability of vGlut2BF activation to suppress hyperphagia in leptin-deficient mice.

claim: Different vGlut2BF neurons strongly responded to different groups of odors.
source: We found that neurons were fairly unresponsive between odor presentations, and different neurons strongly responded to different groups of odors (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in head-fixed animals shown in Figure 5A.

claim: vGlut2BF neurons responded strongly to aversive odorants including butyric acid and 2-methylbutylamine.
source: Interestingly, these same neurons also responded strongly to the two aversive odorants (Figure 5A,B,C), and overall a greater percentage of vGlut2BF neurons were responsive to the aversive odorants compared to food and/or control stimuli (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5A-D comparing responses to different odorants.

claim: A greater percentage of vGlut2BF neurons were responsive to aversive odorants compared to food and/or control stimuli.
source: Interestingly, these same neurons also responded strongly to the two aversive odorants (Figure 5A,B,C), and overall a greater percentage of vGlut2BF neurons were responsive to the aversive odorants compared to food and/or control stimuli (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: vGlut2BF neurons represent a heterogenous population of neurons capable of responding to diverse odors with different valences.
source: Together, these data indicate that vGlut2BF neurons represent a heterogenous population of neurons capable of responding to diverse odors with different valences, and that a greater number of the cells more robustly respond to aversive odorants.
evidence: Inference based on the differential responses to food odors versus aversive odorants shown in Figure 5.

claim: Approximately 10% of patched vGlut2BF neurons received fast, monosynaptic, nicotinic currents from cholinergic neurons.
source: When performing whole-cell recordings from red labeled vGlut2BF neurons while simultaneously photostimulating cholinergic inputs, we found that approximately 10% of patched vGlut2BF neurons received fast, monosynaptic, nicotinic currents (six nicotinic responses from 52 recordings) (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic-assisted electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: Photo-evoked currents from cholinergic neurons onto vGlut2BF neurons were blocked by the nAChR-specific antagonist mecamylamine.
source: In the presence of TTX and 4-AP, photo-evoked currents were blocked by the nAChR-specific antagonist mecamylamine, whereas the mAChR-specific antagonist atropine did not affect photo-evoked post-synaptic responses (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by pharmacology data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The mAChR-specific antagonist atropine did not affect photo-evoked post-synaptic responses from cholinergic neurons onto vGlut2BF neurons.
source: In the presence of TTX and 4-AP, photo-evoked currents were blocked by the nAChR-specific antagonist mecamylamine, whereas the mAChR-specific antagonist atropine did not affect photo-evoked post-synaptic responses (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by pharmacology data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A subset of cholinergic basal forebrain neurons are capable of acting via fast nicotinic signaling onto vGlut2BF neurons to potentially influence appetite suppression.
source: Together, these data suggest that a subset of cholinergic basal forebrain neurons are capable of acting via fast nicotinic signaling onto vGlut2BF neurons, to potentially influence appetite suppression.
evidence: Inference based on the electrophysiology data showing nicotinic currents and the known role of cholinergic neurons in appetite suppression.

claim: vGlut2BF neurons project densely to the lateral hypothalamus.
source: We observed dense projections to the lateral hypothalamus, with no GFP fluorescence in nearby structures such as the paraventricular nucleus or fornix (Figure 7B), as previously described (Do et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by synaptophysin tracing data shown in Figure 7B and citation to Do et al., 2016.

claim: vGlut2BF neurons show no GFP fluorescence in nearby structures such as the paraventricular nucleus or fornix.
source: We observed dense projections to the lateral hypothalamus, with no GFP fluorescence in nearby structures such as the paraventricular nucleus or fornix (Figure 7B), as previously described (Do et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by synaptophysin tracing data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Other prominent regions where vGlut2BF neuron terminal fields were identified include the piriform cortex, olfactory bulb, lateral habenula, and ventral tegmental area.
source: Other prominent regions where we identified terminal fields included the piriform cortex, olfactory bulb, lateral habenula, and ventral tegmental area (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by synaptophysin tracing data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Stimulation of vGlut2BF nerve terminals in the LH resulted in monosynaptic glutamatergic neurotransmission onto vGlut2LH neurons in approximately 88% of cells recorded.
source: Through optogenetic mapping, and in the presence of TTX and 4-AP, we found that stimulation of vGlut2BF nerve terminals in the LH resulted in monosynaptic glutamatergic neurotransmission onto vGlut2LH neurons in approximately 88% of cells recorded (8 out of 9 cells recorded) (Figure 7D–E).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic-assisted electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7D-E.

claim: vGlut2BF neurons directly link to vGlut2LH neurons as a possible upstream circuit node to control appetite suppression.
source: These data directly link vGlut2BF neurons to previously reported vGlut2LH neurons as a possible upstream circuit node to control appetite suppression.
evidence: Inference based on the functional connectivity data and previous literature on vGlut2LH neurons.

claim: Both BF and LH photo-stimulation resulted in approximately fifty percent reduction of food intake compared to unstimulated control conditions.
source: Compared to unstimulated control conditions, both BF and LH photo-stimulation resulted in approximately fifty percent reduction of food intake (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic food intake data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Increasing BF photo-stimulation frequencies led to a further reduction in food intake.
source: Increasing BF photo-stimulation frequencies led to a further reduction in food intake (Figure 8D), whereas photostimulation did not change the amount of food consumed by control GFP injected animals (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by frequency-dependent optogenetic data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Photostimulation did not change the amount of food consumed by control GFP injected animals.
source: Increasing BF photo-stimulation frequencies led to a further reduction in food intake (Figure 8D), whereas photostimulation did not change the amount of food consumed by control GFP injected animals (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by control data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The lateral hypothalamic projections of vGlut2BF neurons mediate appetite suppression.
source: Together, results from these optogentic experiments corroborate findings from chronic activation mNaChBac, and further implicate the lateral hypothalamic projections of VGlut2BF neurons in mediating appetite suppression.
evidence: Inference based on the optogenetic stimulation of LH terminals reducing food intake.

claim: Experimental ChR2 animals tended to avoid food pellets during periods of photostimulation.
source: Interestingly, while performing these manipulations, we observed that experimental ChR2 animals tended to avoid food pellets during periods of photostimulation, while control GFP animals would spend most of their time eating during photostimulation, as would be expected following a 24 hr fasting period.
evidence: Observational data during optogenetic experiments.

claim: Control GFP animals would spend most of their time eating during photostimulation, as would be expected following a 24 hr fasting period.
source: Interestingly, while performing these manipulations, we observed that experimental ChR2 animals tended to avoid food pellets during periods of photostimulation, while control GFP animals would spend most of their time eating during photostimulation, as would be expected following a 24 hr fasting period.
evidence: Observational data during optogenetic experiments.

claim: Fasted control animals spent most of the monitored time near and/or eating food pellets, and very little time in the non-food corner.
source: Whereas fasted control animals spent most of the monitored time near and/or eating food pellets, and very little time in the non-food corner, experimental animals with optogenetic stimulation of vGlut2BF neurons showed a strong avoidance to areas of the arena that harbored food (Figure 9A–B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 9A-B.

claim: Experimental animals with optogenetic stimulation of vGlut2BF neurons showed a strong avoidance to areas of the arena that harbored food.
source: Whereas fasted control animals spent most of the monitored time near and/or eating food pellets, and very little time in the non-food corner, experimental animals with optogenetic stimulation of vGlut2BF neurons showed a strong avoidance to areas of the arena that harbored food (Figure 9A–B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 9A-B.

claim: Prolonged photo-stimulation of either the basal forebrain or the terminal projection field within the lateral hypothalamus led to a preference for the non-food corner.
source: In fact, prolonged photo-stimulation of either the basal forebrain, or the terminal projection field within the lateral hypothalamus, led to a preference for the non-food corner (Figure 9A–B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 9A-B.

claim: Fasted GFP injected animals showed no preference to the non-food corner and spent the majority of their time interacting with food.
source: Notably, fasted GFP injected animals showed no preference to the non-food corner and spent the majority of their time interacting with food (Figure 9A–B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 9A-B.

claim: The induced hypophagia elicited by targeted activation of vGlut2BF neurons or their projections to LH may be attributed to a circuit-specific food avoidance.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that the induced hypophagia elicited by targeted activation of vGlut2BF neurons or their projections to LH, may be attributed to a circuit-specific food avoidance.
evidence: Inference based on the food avoidance behavior observed during optogenetic stimulation.

claim: Photostimulation of vGlut2BF neurons or their LH projections during odor perception of food-associated R-limonene led to a potent food-odor avoidance behavior.
source: Together, these data indicate that photostimulation alone does not cause mice to prefer an empty corner (S-limonene experiment), and that photostimulation of vGlut2BF neurons or their projections to the LH during odor perception of food (R-limonene) can lead to a potent food-odor avoidance behavior.
evidence: Supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 10A-B comparing R-limonene and S-limonene conditions.

claim: Photostimulation alone does not cause mice to prefer an empty corner.
source: Together, these data indicate that photostimulation alone does not cause mice to prefer an empty corner (S-limonene experiment), and that photostimulation of vGlut2BF neurons or their projections to the LH during odor perception of food (R-limonene) can lead to a potent food-odor avoidance behavior.
evidence: Supported by the S-limonene control experiment shown in Figure 10A-B.

claim: Cholinergic basal forebrain neurons have been shown to suppress appetite.
source: Recent work has implicated discrete cell types in the basal forebrain as potent regulators of appetite and feeding. Cholinergic basal forebrain neurons have been shown to suppress appetite, while inhibitory VGAT-positive and somatostatin positive neurons promote general and high caloric food intake, respectively (Herman et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Herman et al., 2016 and Zhu et al., 2017.

claim: Inhibitory VGAT-positive neurons in the basal forebrain promote general food intake.
source: Recent work has implicated discrete cell types in the basal forebrain as potent regulators of appetite and feeding. Cholinergic basal forebrain neurons have been shown to suppress appetite, while inhibitory VGAT-positive and somatostatin positive neurons promote general and high caloric food intake, respectively (Herman et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Herman et al., 2016 and Zhu et al., 2017.

claim: Somatostatin positive neurons in the basal forebrain promote high caloric food intake.
source: Recent work has implicated discrete cell types in the basal forebrain as potent regulators of appetite and feeding. Cholinergic basal forebrain neurons have been shown to suppress appetite, while inhibitory VGAT-positive and somatostatin positive neurons promote general and high caloric food intake, respectively (Herman et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Herman et al., 2016 and Zhu et al., 2017.

claim: Basal forebrain vGlut2+ excitatory neurons are extremely potent suppressors of appetite.
source: Here, we uncovered a previously unknown population of basal forebrain vGlut2 +excitatory neurons as extremely potent suppressors of appetite, some of which receive input from neighboring cholinergic neurons.
evidence: Supported by the mNaChBac activation experiments showing severe hypophagia and starvation.

claim: Some vGlut2BF neurons receive input from neighboring cholinergic neurons.
source: Here, we uncovered a previously unknown population of basal forebrain vGlut2 +excitatory neurons as extremely potent suppressors of appetite, some of which receive input from neighboring cholinergic neurons.
evidence: Supported by the electrophysiology data showing nicotinic currents from cholinergic neurons onto vGlut2BF neurons.

claim: A subset of vGlut2BF neurons responded to food-related odors.
source: We also found that a subset of these excitatory neurons responded to food-related odors, and an even larger portion of them responded to odors associated with aversive and/or spoiled food odorants.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data showing responses to food odors.

claim: An even larger portion of vGlut2BF neurons responded to odors associated with aversive and/or spoiled food odorants.
source: We also found that a subset of these excitatory neurons responded to food-related odors, and an even larger portion of them responded to odors associated with aversive and/or spoiled food odorants.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data showing stronger responses to aversive odorants.

claim: By over-activating vGlut2BF neurons, an overriding hypophagic state was induced where a typical rewarding food pellet became unappetizing.
source: Therefore, it is plausible that by over-activating these neurons, we induced an overriding hypophagic state, where a typical rewarding food pellet became unappetizing.
evidence: Speculation based on the observed hypophagia and food avoidance behaviors.

claim: Non-cholinergic cells in the basal forebrain have been found to predict behavioral responses associated with attention.
source: Additionally, non-cholinergic cells in the basal forebrain have been found to predict behavioral responses associated with attention, and their activity can be modulated by multiple sensory stimuli in a time scale of sub-seconds to seconds (Hangya et al., 2015; Harrison et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from Hangya et al., 2015 and Harrison et al., 2016.

claim: Non-cholinergic basal forebrain cell activity can be modulated by multiple sensory stimuli in a time scale of sub-seconds to seconds.
source: Additionally, non-cholinergic cells in the basal forebrain have been found to predict behavioral responses associated with attention, and their activity can be modulated by multiple sensory stimuli in a time scale of sub-seconds to seconds (Hangya et al., 2015; Harrison et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from Hangya et al., 2015 and Harrison et al., 2016.

claim: vGlut2BF neurons were responsive to cues harboring both positive or negative valences, which would be important responses in an attentive state.
source: Our imaging data support these claims as vGlut2BF neurons were responsive to cues harboring both positive or negative valences, which would be important responses in an attentive state.
evidence: Inference based on the calcium imaging data showing responses to diverse odors.

claim: Nicotine is a potent appetite suppressor.
source: Nicotine is a potent appetite suppressor (Stojakovic et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Stojakovic et al., 2017.

claim: Nicotinic signaling suppresses appetite through POMC neuron activation within the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus.
source: Recent work has identified key roles for nicotinic signaling in suppressing appetite through POMC neuron activation within the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (Mineur et al., 2011; Picciotto et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from Mineur et al., 2011 and Picciotto et al., 2012.

claim: vGlut2BF neurons functionally express acetylcholine nicotinic receptors and provide an additional target by which exogenous nicotine could suppress appetite through extra-hypothalamic neurons.
source: Our electrophysiology results indicate that vGlut2BF neurons functionally express acetylcholine nicotinic receptors, and thus provide an additional target by which exogenous nicotine could suppress appetite through extra-hypothalamic neurons.
evidence: Inference based on the electrophysiology data showing nicotinic currents onto vGlut2BF neurons.

claim: Chronic hyperactivation of vGlut2BF neurons led to drastic hypophagia.
source: Chronic hyperactivation of vGlut2BF neurons led to drastic hypophagia, and acute optogenetic activation of these neurons both reduced food intake and caused avoidance of food and food-associated odors.
evidence: Supported by mNaChBac and optogenetic experiments.

claim: Acute optogenetic activation of vGlut2BF neurons both reduced food intake and caused avoidance of food and food-associated odors.
source: Chronic hyperactivation of vGlut2BF neurons led to drastic hypophagia, and acute optogenetic activation of these neurons both reduced food intake and caused avoidance of food and food-associated odors.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic experiments showing reduced food intake and avoidance behaviors.

claim: Dramatic hypophagia has previously been reported in models of lateral hypothalamic lesions.
source: Such dramatic hypophagia has previously been reported in models of lateral hypothalamic lesions, permanent AgRP neuron ablation in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus, and permanent loss of GABA signaling from AgRP neurons (Gropp et al., 2005; Luquet et al., 2005; Tong et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from Gropp et al., 2005; Luquet et al., 2005; Tong et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2009.

claim: Dramatic hypophagia has previously been reported in models of permanent AgRP neuron ablation in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus.
source: Such dramatic hypophagia has previously been reported in models of lateral hypothalamic lesions, permanent AgRP neuron ablation in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus, and permanent loss of GABA signaling from AgRP neurons (Gropp et al., 2005; Luquet et al., 2005; Tong et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from Gropp et al., 2005; Luquet et al., 2005; Tong et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2009.

claim: Dramatic hypophagia has previously been reported in models of permanent loss of GABA signaling from AgRP neurons.
source: Such dramatic hypophagia has previously been reported in models of lateral hypothalamic lesions, permanent AgRP neuron ablation in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus, and permanent loss of GABA signaling from AgRP neurons (Gropp et al., 2005; Luquet et al., 2005; Tong et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from Gropp et al., 2005; Luquet et al., 2005; Tong et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2009.

claim: The current study is the first instance of a model with precisely targeted manipulations to the basal forebrain that leads to hypophagia and starvation.
source: To our knowledge, the current study is the first instance of a model with precisely targeted manipulations to the basal forebrain that leads to hypophagia and starvation.
evidence: Claim based on comparison with existing literature.

claim: The dramatic phenotype of precipitous weight loss and complete appetite suppression within days of viral mNaChBac expression indicates the high sensitivity of vGlut2BF neuronal firing.
source: The dramatic phenotype of precipitous weight loss and complete appetite suppression within days of viral mNaChBac expression, indicates the high sensitivity of vGlut2BF neuronal firing.
evidence: Inference based on the rapid onset of the phenotype following mNaChBac expression.

claim: Small changes in the excitability of vGlut2BF neurons could have chronic phenotypes in altering feeding behaviors.
source: Given the sensitivity of this neuronal population and the correlated phenotype, it could be possible that small changes in the excitability of this neuronal population could have chronic phenotypes in altering feeding behaviors.
evidence: Speculation based on the observed sensitivity of vGlut2BF neurons.

claim: The resistance of the hypophagic phenotype in leptin deficient mice indicates the feeding pathways altered by vGlut2BF manipulation are either downstream or in parallel to leptin signaling.
source: Furthermore, the resistance of the phenotype in leptin deficient mice indicates the feeding pathways altered by our manipulation are either downstream or in parallel to leptin signaling, but capable of overriding leptin deficient induced hyperphagia.
evidence: Inference based on the Lepob/ob experiments showing suppression of hyperphagia.

claim: The feeding pathways altered by vGlut2BF manipulation are capable of overriding leptin deficient induced hyperphagia.
source: Furthermore, the resistance of the phenotype in leptin deficient mice indicates the feeding pathways altered by our manipulation are either downstream or in parallel to leptin signaling, but capable of overriding leptin deficient induced hyperphagia.
evidence: Supported by the Lepob/ob experiments showing suppression of hyperphagia.

claim: The hypophagic phenotype seen with vGlut2BF activation is similar to that observed with AgRP neuron ablation.
source: Importantly, the hypophagic phenotype seen here is similar to that observed with AgRP neuron ablation, suggesting that the activity of vGlut2BF neurons is a fundamental regulator of feeding behavior (Gropp et al., 2005, p. 2005; Luquet et al., 2005).
evidence: Comparison with cited literature on AgRP neuron ablation.

claim: The activity of vGlut2BF neurons is a fundamental regulator of feeding behavior.
source: Importantly, the hypophagic phenotype seen here is similar to that observed with AgRP neuron ablation, suggesting that the activity of vGlut2BF neurons is a fundamental regulator of feeding behavior (Gropp et al., 2005, p. 2005; Luquet et al., 2005).
evidence: Inference based on the severity of the hypophagic phenotype and comparison with AgRP neuron ablation.

claim: Moderately obese Lepob/ob animals survived AgRP neuron ablation.
source: Further, moderately obese Lepob/ob animals survived AgRP neuron ablation (Wu et al., 2012), whereas viral mNaChBac manipulation of vGlut2BF neurons in obese Lepob/ob animals did not rescue prolonged hypophagia and starvation.
evidence: Cited from Wu et al., 2012.

claim: Viral mNaChBac manipulation of vGlut2BF neurons in obese Lepob/ob animals did not rescue prolonged hypophagia and starvation.
source: Further, moderately obese Lepob/ob animals survived AgRP neuron ablation (Wu et al., 2012), whereas viral mNaChBac manipulation of vGlut2BF neurons in obese Lepob/ob animals did not rescue prolonged hypophagia and starvation.
evidence: Supported by the Lepob/ob experiments showing continued hypophagia.

claim: VGAT-positive inhibitory neurons in the LH have been shown to promote feeding.
source: Genetic subpopulations in the lateral hypothalamus (LH) have been extensively studied for their role in feeding related behavior. VGAT-positive inhibitory neurons in the LH have been shown to promote feeding (Jennings et al., 2015), while vGlut2 positive neurons in the LH elicit food aversion (Jennings et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from Jennings et al., 2015.

claim: vGlut2 positive neurons in the LH elicit food aversion.
source: Genetic subpopulations in the lateral hypothalamus (LH) have been extensively studied for their role in feeding related behavior. VGAT-positive inhibitory neurons in the LH have been shown to promote feeding (Jennings et al., 2015), while vGlut2 positive neurons in the LH elicit food aversion (Jennings et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from Jennings et al., 2013.

claim: vGlut2BF neurons form direct synaptic connections onto vGlut2 positive neurons in the LH.
source: We revealed that vGlut2BF neurons form direct synaptic connections onto vGlut2 positive neurons in the LH, and that their signaling onto LH neurons also diminished food intake and lead to food avoidance, thereby aligning with the previously proposed roles for the lateral hypothalamus.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic-assisted electrophysiology data.

claim: vGlut2BF signaling onto LH neurons diminished food intake and led to food avoidance.
source: We revealed that vGlut2BF neurons form direct synaptic connections onto vGlut2 positive neurons in the LH, and that their signaling onto LH neurons also diminished food intake and lead to food avoidance, thereby aligning with the previously proposed roles for the lateral hypothalamus.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic stimulation of LH terminals reducing food intake and causing avoidance.

claim: Lateral hypothalamic projections to the lateral habenula modulate rewarding aspects of food intake.
source: Previous work has shown that lateral hypothalamic projections to the lateral habenula modulate rewarding aspects of food intake, and that basal forebrain projections to the lateral habenula by somatostatin-expressing neurons can also regulate the rewarding aspects of feeding (Stamatakis et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Stamatakis et al., 2016 and Zhu et al., 2017.

claim: Basal forebrain projections to the lateral habenula by somatostatin-expressing neurons can regulate the rewarding aspects of feeding.
source: Previous work has shown that lateral hypothalamic projections to the lateral habenula modulate rewarding aspects of food intake, and that basal forebrain projections to the lateral habenula by somatostatin-expressing neurons can also regulate the rewarding aspects of feeding (Stamatakis et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Stamatakis et al., 2016 and Zhu et al., 2017.

claim: The lateral habenula has been implicated in reward-related and aversive behaviors through indirect inhibition of the ventral tegmental area (VTA) dopaminergic neurons.
source: The lateral habenula has been implicated in reward-related and aversive behaviors through indirect inhibition of the ventral tegmental area (VTA) dopaminergic neurons, which is another projection site of vGlut2BF neurons.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about lateral habenula function.

claim: The VTA is a projection site of vGlut2BF neurons.
source: The lateral habenula has been implicated in reward-related and aversive behaviors through indirect inhibition of the ventral tegmental area (VTA) dopaminergic neurons, which is another projection site of vGlut2BF neurons.
evidence: Supported by synaptophysin tracing data showing VTA projections.

claim: vGlut2BF neurons could play a pivotal role in encoding the rewarding aspects of food intake.
source: Therefore, given the interconnected nature of cell types between these structures, vGlut2BF neurons could also play a pivotal role in encoding the rewarding aspects of food intake.
evidence: Speculation based on the projection patterns and known functions of target regions.

claim: Other nodes in the vGlut2BF circuit are important since lateral hypothalamic stimulation of vGlut2BF terminals did not fully recapitulate the avoidance behavior seen when vGlut2BF cell bodies were stimulated.
source: Based on cell-body versus LH projection stimulation results, other nodes in this circuit are clearly important since lateral hypothalamic stimulation of vGlut2BF terminals did not fully recapitulate the avoidance behavior seen when vGlut2BF cell bodies were stimulated (Figures 8, 9 and 10).
evidence: Inference based on comparing the magnitude of effects between cell body and terminal stimulation.

claim: vGlut2 neurons in the medial septum reduced food intake through paraventricular hypothalamic projections.
source: Recent investigations in the medial septum (MS) have also revealed neuronal populations that are capable of influencing feeding (Sweeney et al., 2017; Sweeney and Yang, 2016). Importantly, vGlut2 neurons in the MS reduced food intake through paraventricular hypothalamic projections, but to date, have not been shown to synapse onto lateral hypothalamic neurons (Sweeney et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Sweeney et al., 2017.

claim: vGlut2 neurons in the medial septum have not been shown to synapse onto lateral hypothalamic neurons.
source: Recent investigations in the medial septum (MS) have also revealed neuronal populations that are capable of influencing feeding (Sweeney et al., 2017; Sweeney and Yang, 2016). Importantly, vGlut2 neurons in the MS reduced food intake through paraventricular hypothalamic projections, but to date, have not been shown to synapse onto lateral hypothalamic neurons (Sweeney et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Sweeney et al., 2017.

claim: Anterograde tracing highlighted an absence of vGlut2BF neuron innervation to the paraventricular hypothalamus.
source: Additionally, anterograde tracing highlighted an absence of vGlut2BF neuron innervation to the paraventricular hypothalamus.
evidence: Supported by synaptophysin tracing data showing no GFP fluorescence in the PVN.

claim: Excitatory neurons in the MS were identified to influence auditory and somatosensory cue-based avoidance through lateral habenula projections.
source: Excitatory neurons in the MS were also recently identified to influence auditory and somatosensory cue-based avoidance through lateral habenula projections (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: MS excitatory neurons have a unique locomotor phenotype attributed to projections to the preoptic region.
source: That study also identified a unique locomotor phenotype, attributed to MS excitatory neuron projections to the preoptic region.
evidence: Cited from Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: Photostimulation of excitatory-neuron cell bodies in the DBB did not result in changes in locomotion.
source: Importantly, when we photostimulated excitatory-neuron cell bodies in the DBB, we did not observe any changes in locomotion, nor did we see increased cellular activity by calcium imaging when head-fixed animals moved on a walking ball.
evidence: Observational data during optogenetic and calcium imaging experiments.

claim: vGlut2BF neurons did not show increased cellular activity by calcium imaging when head-fixed animals moved on a walking ball.
source: Importantly, when we photostimulated excitatory-neuron cell bodies in the DBB, we did not observe any changes in locomotion, nor did we see increased cellular activity by calcium imaging when head-fixed animals moved on a walking ball.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: vGlut2BF neurons cause an avoidance phenotype due to food olfactory sensory cues.
source: Additionally, our data indicate vGlut2BF neurons cause an avoidance phenotype due to food olfactory sensory cues.
evidence: Supported by the food-odor avoidance experiments with R-limonene.

claim: vGlut2 neurons in the medial septum and the diagonal band of Broca represent unique basal forebrain populations with distinct projections that mediate appetite suppressing roles.
source: Together, these studies suggest that vGlut2 neurons in the medial septum and the diagonal band of Broca represent unique basal forebrain populations with distinct projections that mediate appetite suppressing roles.
evidence: Inference based on comparing the current study with studies on MS vGlut2 neurons.

claim: The DBB of the basal forebrain is not considered a primary sensory cortex for olfactory information.
source: Additionally, the DBB of the basal forebrain is not considered a primary sensory cortex for olfactory information, and therefore the function of other presynaptic inputs onto vGlut2BF neurons need to be further investigated to understand how more complex cognitive states can utilize sensory cues to suppress appetite.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about brain anatomy and function.

claim: Pre-synaptic tracing onto vGlut2BF neurons highlights the orbitofrontal and agranular insular cortex as potential targets which could integrate sensory perception and higher level cognition to suppress appetite through basal forebrain circuitry.
source: Pre-synaptic tracing onto vGlut2BF neurons highlight the orbitofrontal and agranular insular cortex as potential targets which could integrate sensory perception and higher level cognition to suppress appetite through basal forebrain circuitry (Do et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from Do et al., 2016.

claim: Sensory perception of food can induce salivation, increase appetite, and prepare the body for food intake through the release of gastric acid and insulin prior to consumption.
source: Sensory perception of food can induce salivation, increase appetite, and prepare the body for food intake through the release of gastric acid and insulin prior to consumption (Rogers and Hill, 1989).
evidence: Cited from Rogers and Hill, 1989.

claim: The perception of rotting or spoiled food can elicit diminished appetite and overt food aversion.
source: Similarly, the perception of rotting or spoiled food can elicit the opposite effect, including diminished appetite and overt food aversion (Li and Liberles, 2015).
evidence: Cited from Li and Liberles, 2015.

claim: The integration of sensory information to either drive or diminish appetite involves a complex combination of both innate and learned behaviors.
source: The integration of sensory information to either drive or diminish appetite involves a complex combination of both innate and learned behaviors (Li and Liberles, 2015; Rozin and Fallon, 1987).
evidence: Cited from Li and Liberles, 2015 and Rozin and Fallon, 1987.

claim: Food perception can be interpreted as a higher-cortical function, beyond the level of hypothalamic feeding centers.
source: Food perception can thus be interpreted as a higher-cortical function, beyond the level of hypothalamic feeding centers, and necessarily requires communication between hypothalamic circuits and extra-hypothalamic regions.
evidence: Inference based on the complexity of sensory integration and learned behaviors.

claim: Hypothalamic feeding-associated neurons are rapidly modulated by sensory perception of food prior to consummatory behaviors.
source: Previous research has shown that hypothalamic feeding-associated neurons are rapidly modulated by sensory perception of food prior to consummatory behaviors (Betley et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Betley et al., 2015 and Chen et al., 2015.

claim: Neurons within the lateral hypothalamus have been shown to rapidly drive both appetitive and aversive feeding behaviors.
source: Additionally, nearby neurons within the lateral hypothalamus have also been shown to rapidly drive both appetitive and aversive feeding behaviors (Jennings et al., 2015; Jennings et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from Jennings et al., 2015 and Jennings et al., 2013.

claim: Anosmic humans exhibit abnormal food perception and changes in appetite.
source: In humans and rodents, olfaction plays a key sensory perceptive role in feeding. Anosmic humans exhibit abnormal food perception and changes in appetite (Bonfils et al., 2005).
evidence: Cited from Bonfils et al., 2005.

claim: Olfaction in mice has been shown to impact food intake and metabolism.
source: Similarly, olfaction in mice has been shown to impact food intake and metabolism (Riera et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Riera et al., 2017.

claim: Olfactory perception of food has been shown to affect neuronal activity in hypothalamic feeding centers.
source: Additionally, olfactory perception of food itself has been shown to affect neuronal activity in hypothalamic feeding centers (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Chen et al., 2015.

claim: The basal forebrain has been shown to mediate aspects of wakefulness, attention, learning and plasticity, and sensory modulation.
source: Traditionally identified as a cholinergic center, the basal forebrain has been shown to mediate aspects of wakefulness, attention, learning and plasticity, and sensory modulation (Golden et al., 2016; Hangya et al., 2015; Harrison et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2015; Pinto et al., 2013; Ramanathan et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Golden et al., 2016; Hangya et al., 2015; Harrison et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2015; Pinto et al., 2013; Ramanathan et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2015.

claim: The cholinergic basal forebrain has been identified as a robust modulator of appetite.
source: Recent work, has also identified the cholinergic basal forebrain as a robust modulator of appetite (Herman et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Herman et al., 2016 and Zhu et al., 2017.

claim: vGlut2BF neurons promote wakefulness and exhibit diverse activation patterns in response to behavioral and training tasks.
source: Data have shown that vGlut2BF neurons promote wakefulness, and exhibit diverse activation patterns in response to behavioral and training tasks (Harrison et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Harrison et al., 2016 and Xu et al., 2015.

claim: Odors associated with rotten food and aversive odorant signaling through trace-amine-associated receptors in the main olfactory bulb potently activated vGlut2BF neurons.
source: Further in vivo microendoscopic imaging revealed that both odors associated with rotten food, and aversive odorant signaling through trace-amine-associated receptors in the main olfactory bulb (Dewan et al., 2013; Osada et al., 2018; Saraiva et al., 2016) potently activated vGlut2BF neurons.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data and citations to Dewan et al., 2013; Osada et al., 2018; Saraiva et al., 2016.

claim: Optogenetic activation of vGlut2BF cell bodies or their hypothalamic projections was sufficient to induce hypophagia and led to food avoidance upon the olfactory perception of food.
source: Furthermore, optogenetic activation of vGlut2BF cell bodies or their hypothalamic projections was sufficient to induce hypophagia and led to food avoidance upon the olfactory perception of food.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic experiments showing reduced food intake and avoidance behaviors.

claim: vGlut2BF neurons comprise an odor-responsive excitatory neuronal population that projects to the lateral hypothalamus and is capable of reducing feeding behavior by modulating avoidance to food and/or food-related odors.
source: Together, these data reveal that vGlut2BF neurons comprise an odor-responsive excitatory neuronal population that projects to the lateral hypothalamus and is capable of reducing feeding behavior by modulating avoidance to food and/or food-related odors.
evidence: Summary inference based on all experimental data presented in the study.
